To tackle complex music composition, we introduce a novel approach called Pied Piper, which draws from advanced language models to create a strong foundation for music generation through limited and targeted text inputs. This approach is particularly well-suited for producing short music segments with precise specifications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Pied Piper by developing a simple web application that leverages these concepts, resulting in engaging music compositions in multiple styles. This approach and the application code are available for public use.

We establish a local concept of geometric framework on Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, which can be seen as a local version of the concept for presheaves on Lie groupoids and stacks. This construction is highly effective for categories of objects with significant symmetry, where it enables the creation of geometric framework members that respect this symmetry. To demonstrate its utility, we show that by applying this construction to Lie groupoids, we obtain a solution to a problem posed by the second-named author in reference [19].

A candidate massive star nursery, IRDC G339.872-0.043, has been undergoing core formation for an estimated 5000 years.  Observations of this complex infrared dark cloud reveal three separate core prototypes.  Core prototypes within IRDC G339.872-0.043 are thought to have the potential to give rise to massive star formation.  A comparison with the L1527 model suggests that the dust and gas properties in IRDC G339.872-0..043 can be found in the early stages of core formation, specifically in protostellar stages.  Protostellar stages in IRDC G339.872-0.043 exhibit increased gas temperatures and peak densities compared to the L1527 model.  A duration of about 5000 years is needed for cores to progress from the stage similar to L1527 to the stage similar to TMC-1 S.  Core prototypes in IRDC G339.872-0.043 have already spent about 5000 years in core formation stage.  They are now at a stage similar to TMC-1 S where multiple cores are developing and expanding in different dimensions.  It is expected that in about 0.01 Myr from now, the core prototypes in IRDC G339.872-0.043 will give rise to massive star formation.

Godel modal logics fall within the family of intermediate logics, which incorporate modalities from intuitionistic and classical logic. These logics can be expanded to include axioms like distributivity, congruence, and prelinearity. This study examines relational structures and associative semigroups as Godel modal logic frameworks, leveraging the zig-zag law to link these frameworks. It is demonstrated that certain associative semigroups provide a suitable framework for various extensions of Godel modal logics, specifically those based on distributive, congruence, and prelinear logic. These associations between logic and mathematics also spark an interest in investigating relational structures and semigroups based on finite or infinite trees.

LiDAR systems are widely used for gathering detailed information about 3D environments, which is then utilized to create high-quality road maps and scenarios for autonomous vehicles. These 3D point clouds are composed of numerous unlabelled points, each representing a specific location and aspect of a real-world scene. In contrast to autonomous systems powered by 2D images or lidar intensity data, 3D point clouds offer more comprehensive data about the environment. Our research aims to explore the potential of LiDAR-based 3D point clouds as a primary source of information for autonomous vehicles by leveraging the advantages of higher-dimensional data. We utilize a unique dataset consisting of 3D point clouds and corresponding labels for classification and grouping, which we incorporate into a robust evaluation framework that assesses the efficacy of both traditional and cutting-edge machine learning approaches. Our results indicate that cutting-edge 3D machine learning models exhibit exceptional performance on complex classification tasks and the ability to derive meaningful representations of 3D data. Furthermore, our research reveals that sophisticated 3D models can offer substantial improvements over baseline LiDAR-based methods and paves the way for future studies to further examine the capabilities and limitations of LiDAR-based 3D point clouds as a foundation for autonomous vehicles.

We derive explicit formulas for calculating geometrically mean values of functionals of integrals of random fields on the sphere, specifically for Zernike polynomials. This involves converting the polynomials into Laplace polynomials and utilizing the properties of special functions. The obtained formulas demonstrate a recursive structure. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the standard and non-standard Zernike recurrence formulas. The formulation is applicable to fields following non-isotropic gamma distributions.

The observation of neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic particles has been documented over several decades. Research indicates that neutrino flux originates from the detection of neutrinos interacting with matter, whereas ultra-high-energy cosmic particles lack clear evidence of their sources. Both phenomena exhibit correlation with the arrival directions of high-energy cosmic rays. Analyzing the connection between neutrino and UHECR fluxes, considering spatial and energetic ties, may reveal the origin of these high-energy phenomena. This research focuses on the examination of neutrino and UHECR flux relationships, especially in the UHECR multiplicity increase observed in neutrino flux maxima at very high energies.

The flow of liquid foams is significantly influenced by two main factors: the arrangement of bubbles and the nature of the liquid surface. Despite this dual influence, researchers have focused mostly on the geometric structure of the bubbles when studying the flow. In contrast, this study reveals the crucial role that surface tension plays in the flow by transferring stress laterally across the liquid surface. The transferred stress is shown to be the same as the shear stress experienced by the bulk liquid, which is the result of the liquid's viscosity multiplied by the shear rate. However, this transferred stress has a critical limit, beyond which it disrupts the stability of the foam surface, leading to stick-slip behavior during flow. This phenomenon is seen in both thin and thick foams, although it occurs at vastly different shear rates due to the difference in liquid surface relaxation times.

This study employs a unique combination of topological feature extraction and an efficient neural network to develop a more effective and efficient method for identifying skin carcinomas. The proposed approach utilizes entropy as a criterion to select a limited number of high-quality, diverse samples for each class, thereby reducing the impact of outlier samples on the neural network's training. A comparative analysis of the proposed method with existing techniques was conducted using the widely used HMISC dataset, resulting in significant improvements in accuracy, sensitivity, and the AUC score. Furthermore, the proposed approach demonstrated robustness in optimizing model performance with the training data itself.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a confined cell leads to
the creation of intricate finger patterns as an invasive fluid displaces the
more dense fluid within the cell. Due to the presence of both effects, the
character of these patterns becomes highly versatile and ultimately decides the
shape of the resulting interface. Despite being critically influenced by the
transition from laminar to turbulent flow, the dynamics of this choice remains
largely unclear and cannot be accurately predicted by existing theories, as
even the transition itself is greatly extended by the low Reynolds numbers
within this experiment. Through the observation of both the beginning and the
eventual stages of this process, we have the opportunity to evaluate the role
of both surface tension and friction in governing the development of the flow,
as well as the formation of the finger patterns, as they transition from a
dominated-by-surface-tension state to one dominated by friction.

Initial conditions play a crucial role in determining the phase space volume in microscopic Hamiltonian systems. Typically, generating an arbitrary phase space volume involves deriving multiple first integrals, which can be challenging to obtain. In certain cases, such as free expansion, a specific initial condition can result in a specific final state, enabling the creation of an arbitrary initial condition. Our study reveals that for the one-dimensional free expansion, multiple initial conditions can lead to a wide range of final states, including those that might initially seem impossible. For example, it can be shown that it's possible to achieve certain final states with very low or very high momenta at specific initial positions, which would typically require precise control of the initial position and momentum. Our analysis indicates that these outcomes are a result of the interplay between the Hamiltonian and potential energy functions, which cause a conspiracy of peaks, allowing for the creation of certain final states that would otherwise defy explanation.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific variants of indenyl and phenyl ethynyl molecules, cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives with an ethynyl group attached to the 5th carbon respectively, towards the TMC-1 direction using the ATLASxtra+ receiver of the MALT telescope at a sensitivity of 1.3 mJy. Their non-circular velocity profiles indicate a velocity shift of approximately -5.5 km/s in relation to the 4.23 km/s profile of CH$_3$OH. The abundance of these phenyl derivatives is found to be significantly lower than that of their cyclopentadiene counterparts, with an estimated ratio of 0.4:1.7 $\times$ 10$^{-9}$ for benzene: cyclopentadiene. This discovery helps bridge the gap between observational data and chemical models of the TMC-1 molecular envelope.

The sequence-to-sequence translation model primarily relies on attention to connect source and target sentence structures, however existing research reveals that the majority of current models suffer from learned attention patterns being overly similar, resulting in them failing to effectively utilize source sentences when translating complex sentences. In response, we introduce a look-forward attention mechanism that not only considers previously explored attention patterns but also allows the model to reference previously derived target language, ultimately aiming to create a more coherent sentence. Experimental results indicate this attention pattern significantly enhances the translation performance, particularly in cases involving complex sentences. In particular, it achieves substantial gains on the multi-source sentence translation task and around a 1% improvement in the WMT2014 English to German translation task.

The success of advanced science projects depends on the seamless interaction of computer experts and researchers from other fields who share a common goal but differ in their skills and programming perspectives. To accelerate the pace of discovery, a technique was developed to translate high-level application frameworks into suitable computational frameworks, allowing them to run efficiently on distributed systems. This technique, known as the Delta4 approach, was initially used to convert military surveillance applications into grid computing protocols. The development of Delta4 was influenced by the desire to address the challenges posed by complex surveillance projects, which involved tackling problems of data overload, unreliable sensors, and malicious threats. However, the same issues also made them suitable for implementation on top of grid computing platforms, which are characterized by fragile nodes, large scales, and unpredictable behavior. Furthermore, the complexity of these applications made them unsuitable for straightforward parallelization, leading to the need for novel translational methods like Delta4. The use of Delta4 resulted in successful, reliable, and high-performance implementations of various applications, which in turn validated the approach. However, the approach has its limitations, which become evident when applying it to systems that are more efficiently designed with inherent support for translation, such as systems built with web services and object-oriented programming.

A combined dark fluid model has been presented that incorporates a dissipative component into the dark energy system, resulting in the emergence of a specific cosmological constant within the framework of general relativity. The model's dynamics were examined using a parametric approach, and its parameters were determined using data from supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and baryon acoustic oscillations. Furthermore, the model was found to comply with the requirements set by the Hubble tension, and its properties were analyzed through a computation of the equation of state coefficient and the spectral index of the scalar perturbation sector. The model's stability was investigated, and it was found that the perturbation analysis yields the same values as the global estimates for the Hubble constant and the density parameter. The model exhibits a unique characteristic where the rate of the cosmic dark matter transition is constant, and it was predicted that a specific ratio of the dark matter density to the dark energy density remains constant at a particular point in time. The model's predictions and the associated mathematical derivations are supported by the currently available observational data.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a desire for personal growth. Unfortunately, many students lack curiosity due to various factors, such as fear of failure or inadequate self-confidence. Unfortunately, curiosity cannot be directly observed as it exists solely in individuals' minds. As a result, there is a lack of effective metrics to measure curiosity in learning environments. To address this gap, we propose a novel, multi-faceted approach to quantify curiosity through a combination of physiological responses and verbal communications. Our methodology leverages advanced technologies, including eye-tracking, brain-wave scanning, and machine learning tools to analyze conversations. We demonstrate the feasibility of this strategy by designing and implementing a data-driven experiment involving 36 students in a learning environment. Our findings show that curiosity can be measured using our proposed methodology and that it has distinct patterns during different learning stages, particularly before introducing new material when curiosity is high and after understanding is reached when curiosity drops. Our research provides a foundation for further exploration into the dynamics of curiosity in learning environments and can be used to develop more effective learning materials and instructional strategies.

This research introduces a novel Gaussian process model, centered on Mat\'ern principles, that can be applied to complex datasets represented as graphs. Unlike current Gaussian process models, which are often limited by their ability to scale efficiently to large datasets, this approach takes advantage of the graph structure to achieve both theoretical convergence guarantees and significant performance improvements in practice. We demonstrate that the proposed model achieves comparable or better accuracy compared to multiple state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmark datasets while significantly outperforming these methods in terms of running time.

The optimal detection method for urban road systems using mobile sensors, such as ridesharing vehicles, is key to maintaining clear traffic information and associated safety standards. A statistical method for identifying road types using sensor data from mobile sensors is proposed, it incorporates utility-based decision making and learns from data through probabilistic modeling. The method determines the most effective sensor deployment strategy to achieve the highest accuracy in road type identification. Experiments using real data from Google Maps and ridesharing vehicle location history demonstrate that the proposed system can accurately identify road types and optimize sensor deployment for reduced costs, also evaluating the impact of relevant factors on system performance.

Our research investigates the significance of neutrino and dark energy sector contributions to the invisible decay of the $J/\psi$ meson. Using the effective field theory approach, we examine how electroweak and quantum fluctuations affect the calculation. Specifically, we focus on the $\gamma + X$ disintegration of the $J/\psi$, where $X$ represents an invisible particle. To determine the significance of new physics terms, we compare them to the standard model prediction by calculating the ratio of the observed and expected low-energy amplitudes. This ratio enables us to establish a relationship between the neutrino and dark energy sector contribution and the $J/\psi$ decay width. By analyzing a vast range of theoretical models, we find that none of them yield a $J/\psi$ width within the experimentally measured range of $e$ or $K$ mesons. However, we find that a substantial number of models containing a dark photon or a dark scalar particle may be confirmed or ruled out by a precise measurement of the $J/\psi\to \text{invisible}$ decay width. Alternatively, a significant number of models based on a dark vector boson or scalar particle may be confirmed or ruled out by a sensitive measurement of the $J/\psi\to \gamma + \text{invisible}$ decay width.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) for time-series data set within multiple dimensional spaces. We further develop a comprehensive framework for applying MFSSA consistently across various domains, thereby enabling a dimension-free framework. This is achieved by utilizing the singular spectrum in each dimensional space, which effectively equates the dimensions. This equivalence facilitates a cross-domain analysis, allowing for a comparison of the spectral components across different dimensions. We subsequently derive the parameters for estimating the MFSSA, along with associated distributions. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we conduct simulation studies in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, we apply the generalised MFSSA approach to examine the daily temperature variations across distinct spatial locations within the United Kingdom during different seasonal periods.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are being widely adopted for their potential to cost savings, consistency, and reduced grading burdens. However, the underlying mechanics of these platforms are often unclear, posing risks to education systems if they yield scores with inherent biases. This research delves into the intricacies of one such platform, the ETS's Advanced Essay Scoring (AES) framework, which we discovered exhibits both unstable responses to significant changes and inadequate reactions to minor modifications. Our findings highlighted scoring inconsistencies when essays were modified by changing the focus on specific aspects, such as shifting from a first-person to a third-person perspective. To address these issues, we employed two methods to refine the AES framework: reducing the representational bias of the essay model by applying adversarial retraining, and incorporating a role-based perspective model to influence the scoring process. Our results showed improved performance of the modified AES framework in evaluating perspectives beyond what was trained for.

This study continues the research on one-dimensional random walks with growing step-size, specifically examining the long-term behavior of the walk's duration on positive intervals. The primary focus is on determining the worst-case scenario for the number of steps required to achieve a given probability threshold of reaching an arbitrary positive interval. This approach enables comparison with existing studies on the walk's cover time or cover time with a focus on specific intervals. In contrast to these studies, the walk's cover time or cover time with a focus on specific intervals does not capture the walk's global persistence on positive intervals, which is the subject of this research.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to mimic the plasma conditions found in an ITER-like device during ELMs. A key component of this facility is the plasma generator, which uses a helicon source to create a constant plasma density of around 1 x 10^19 m^-3 across a 1.5 meter long section of the tube. Due to the limited amount of data available from previous tests, a detailed study was conducted using data from multiple heating powers (0.1 MW to 1 MW) and different tube lengths (0.5 meters to 1.5 meters). These studies revealed that when the plasma generator is operated in helicon mode, it produces a steady plasma density with only minor changes, regardless of the length of the plasma tube. However, it was also found that increasing the heating power does not have a significant impact on plasma density when using two antennas. On a separate note, it was observed that when the heating power is switched between the two antennas, there is a temporary drop in plasma density, which recovers within a few microseconds.

In the context of an ecosystem where a microbial biopesticide is utilized to control invasive species, we examine a systematic approach to model the environment. The model incorporates several key components, including the impact of a suppressive factor on the biopesticide's efficacy and the opposing effects of intraspecific competition on the target species. We analyze the model's equilibrium points and conduct a stability test. Additionally, we investigate the model's results in both theoretical and applied settings, validating our findings numerically. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the dynamic interaction between microbial biopesticides and the environments they target.

In analyzing pathology slides, nucleus segmentation is a crucial preliminary step.
Due to variations in image quality, this task becomes very challenging, especially when
attempting to develop generally applicable algorithms. For example, the presence of
inflammatory cells in bowel tissue samples can hinder nucleus segmentation due to
their differing sizes, shapes, and color intensities. To address this issue, we propose
a novel dual-stage network called W-Net, which first employs a coarse network to
identify potential nucleus locations and then uses a fine network to refine its output
based on these initial predictions. By combining the results from these two stages,
W-Net can produce a complete and accurate nucleus segmentation mask. Unlike
existing cycle-consistency methods that require matching input and output nucleus
masks, W-Net offers several advantages, including enhanced segmentation accuracy
and greater robustness in the face of tissue erosion. Our experimental evaluations
on large datasets have consistently shown significant improvements in nucleus
segmentation accuracy.

Let's consider a field of characteristic not two and denote it by $k$. We establish the converse of the first part of Langlands' classification for the groups $SO(N,K)$ and $Sp(N,K)$ when $N$ is an odd number greater than one. Additionally, this classification holds true in the context of characteristic zero, as demonstrated by Gelauff and Sutherland. Our proof focuses on the representation of generic irreducible objects from the category $R_{\phi}$ in the Langlands parameter set $\Lambda_{irr}(G) \subset \Hom_K(\res_K\phi, k_\phi^\times)$. We achieve this by showing there exists an isomorphism between the irreducible generic representations of $G$ and the maps from $\res_K\phi$ to $k_\phi^\times$ that factor through the map $\phi \circ \eta^{-1}$, where $\eta$ is the non-trivial character from $K^\times$ to $k_\phi^\times$. Furthermore, this classification maintains its validity in the context of positive characteristic, as demonstrated by the work of Diamond and Sasaki.

A graph G is considered to have an detectable hamiltonian property if a hamiltonian cycle can be identified using a specific method. This paper explores the relationship between G and its second iteration, specifically examining which G instances result in an iterated graph that is detectable and has a hamiltonian path from its initial iteration. We discuss various equivalent conditions for this relationship and provide a method for determining these conditions in a practical context.

Cell death through pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to SARS-CoV-2 transmission by facilitating the spread of the virus from one host to another. This process is associated with various clinical symptoms, including coughing, sneezing, and diarrhea that allow the virus to propagate over long distances. We develop a mathematical model to analyze the pyroptotic cell death induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection, considering the roles of host and pathogen factors that initiate and regulate pyroptosis. Our model also explores the effectiveness of anti-inflammatory interventions in slowing down pyroptotic cell death, which could potentially reduce virus transmission.

External influences can enter a reinforcement learning model through its state and reward functions, which may lead to poor performance due to their unknown nature. This problem is addressed by using a process called end-to-end backward identification, which involves analyzing the learned policy to determine the parts of the state and reward that are endogenous to the system. This process is then used to remove the external components from the state and reward, resulting in a simplified version that can be optimized through reward modification or the introduction of an auxiliary reward. This approach is evaluated using multiple examples, which show that it can successfully eliminate the impact of external influences on reinforcement learning systems.

A blockchain-based smart contract platform like Tezos can benefit from a validation tool like HELMHOLTZ, which uses refinement types to ensure contracts meet specified requirements and improve their reliability. By linking Michelson, the programming language used for Tezos contracts, to refinement types, HELMHOLTZ enables the precise verification of these contracts, providing benefits such as more efficient and reliable code, better performance due to reduced execution time, and protection against common errors such as integer overflows. Additionally, the complex type system of HELMHOLTZ helps prevent subtle issues from arising during contract execution.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have been driven by their flexible application to both spatial and temporal network analysis. We believe a key factor behind this success is the matching filter approach, a fundamental concept shared across GCNNs that we will delve into through our analysis of matched temporal graph filtering. This paper presents an in-depth examination of this matching filter idea as the basis of GCNNs, offering a detailed derivation of multiple GCNN variants, including graph convolutional networks, graph recurrent networks, and graph attention networks. Our analysis demonstrates that these networks can be viewed as applying a matched filtering process to identify feature values across neighboring nodes and to determine the weights given to different nodes in a network.

We investigate a simple model that connects gravity to a scalar field via a Chern-Simons action, considering both flat and curved spacetimes. By examining the metric and scalar field equations derived from the Chern-Simons action, we can relate the gravitational field to the scalar field through a gauge field. This connection results in modified Einstein field equations featuring a spin-2 field that arises from the Chern-Simons term. In the case of a static, spherically symmetric black hole or soliton with a non-zero scalar field, the consistency of the Chern-Simons theory demands that the Ricci tensor be identically zero. However, the failure to find smooth, rotating black hole or soliton solutions in general relativity can be attributed to an incorrect assumption that the metric and scalar field are separately flat. Instead, we show that the combination of the metric and scalar field forms an Einstein metric, allowing for the creation of rotating, hairy black hole or soliton solutions in Einstein gravity when a non-Abelian gauge force is present.

We discover a novel class of integrable systems on the sphere with arbitrary genus, defined by a specific type of quadratic exchange matrix. This breakthrough allows us the develop a new approach to studying these systems' properties. Notably, we find that the systems exhibit non-reversible affine symmetry and are closely related to a category of solvable two-dimensional lattices with genus greater than one. These connections enable us to utilize the integral basis representation to classify all the exchangeable systems on the genus-one surface. Furthermore, we establish that the genus-zero case is encompassed by a specific subset of the genus-one models.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of tissue displacement in elastography is crucial for further analysis of tissue properties. The Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique has shown enhancements in beamforming and displacement estimation by creating virtual transducer sources and forming synthetic apertures, ultimately resulting in better lateral resolution and displacement estimation. This study investigates the application of VOSA in elastography by analysing its effects on displacement estimation and performance. Numerical simulations and ultrasound elastography experiments were conducted to examine VOSA's performance. The simulation revealed that VOSA outperformed the conventional techniques with improved displacement estimation and lateral resolution. The experimental results also demonstrated that VOSA yielded better displacement estimation and lateral resolution than the conventional techniques. Furthermore, the comparison of conventional and VOSA-based elastography revealed that VOSA provided more accurate results.

Students learn programming concepts through both code and narrative, with combined approaches often used in tutorial websites, how-to guides, and educational software. Yet, there are no standard frameworks for describing algorithms that incorporate both formal code and narrative explanations. To address this gap, we propose a framework consisting of two components. Firstly, we define a new specification method for algorithm codes using a simple, high-level pseudocode that can be efficiently translated into practical languages. Secondly, we develop a clear, concise language for describing algorithm explanations. We then demonstrate our framework's effectiveness by applying it to a wide range of common algorithms, making these accessible to students through our RationalPseudocode website.

A Boolean algebra $[$\mathbb{B}(x,y)$]$ is a Boolean algebra consisting of the intervals $[x,y]$ within the real line $\mathbb{R}$, with the operations of union and intersection. A subset of points within a Boolean algebra is considered independent if it has the maximum possible size according to the Boolean algebra order, and cannot be expanded further. The independent subsets of a Boolean algebra can be classified into different types, including a type known as the Ramsey type. The Boolean algebra based on the real line has a V-shaped order, and this paper explores the Ramsey characteristics of the independent subsets within this type of Boolean algebra. The paper especially focuses on finding the Ramsey characteristics of the Ramsey types one through six within this Boolean algebra. The paper also presents a method for determining the Ramsey characteristics of the independent subsets within a V-shaped Boolean algebra by using a specific subset of a another V-shaped Boolean algebra.

In the context of high-dimensional data, a new algorithm is introduced for the $k$-means clustering problem. The algorithm, called Dynamic Fault Tolerant K-Means (DFTK), operates within a limited memory capacity and tolerates a limited number of cluster mergers. DFTK is designed to yield a stable estimator for the optimal number of clusters, $k$, and provides a data structure that approximates an optimal clustering according to a fixed $k$. The algorithm's performance is guaranteed to yield a cluster spacing parameter, $\lambda$, indicating the instability present. The review of existing literature reveals that $\lambda$ is not addressed in prior research. Subsequent analysis establishes an lower bound for $\lambda$ in relation to $k$. The novel algorithm is compared to a natural extension of the Fault Tolerant K-Means (FFK) algorithm. The comparison is performed under the condition that initial clustering meets certain requirements. The review of existing technique enables the extension of prior results, and the comparison leads to the conclusion that the DFTK algorithm outperforms FFK in terms of $\lambda$ when $k$ is sufficiently large. The DFTK algorithm is integrated into an online learning framework. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on multiple data sets, and the obtained results are made available. The analysis of DFTK is linked to an related problem known as dynamic $k$-means grouping. A new algorithm, FT K-Means, is introduced

We introduce a hierarchical framework of randomized games that builds upon a fundamental pursuit-evasion problem in discrete spaces. We establish a connection between our hierarchical model and existing applications, showcasing its relevance to optimizing strategies in multi-agent systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that solving the generalized pursuit-evasion problem is computationally feasible by leveraging our hierarchical approach, which involves solving a series of smaller, more manageable problems. Additionally, we examine the theoretical efficiency of our method and compare it to alternative strategies. Our method specifically offers enhanced performance in scenarios where the environment consists of multiple distinct components or 'rooms'.

We examine circular and nontransitive probabilities which arise from circular
permutations of n distinct items and the phenomenon where random selection has
a lower expected value than a fixed item. We investigate the relationship between
these concepts and show that circular probabilities are a subset of transitive
probabilities. We also present a generative model for creating fair distributions
of circular probabilities and use this model to develop new constructions for both
circular and nontransitive probabilities. Additionally, we discuss the relationship
between these probabilities and the geometric shapes formed by their corresponding
orderings.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the current implementation of this method is restricted by the fixed adaptation architecture of the cycleGAN model, which does not allow for a flexible image style transformation, a key characteristic of contrast enhancement. To address this limitation, we present a new cycleGAN variant called AdaIN-Switchable cycleGAN, or AS-cycleGAN, which integrates an adaptive instance normalization layer into both the unsupervised training processes, allowing for both image style transformation and mean-missing value correction. By switching the AdaIN layer's learning mode during training from batch normalization to instance normalization, and vice versa, we found that this strategy yields a more effective and efficient image enhancement result following evaluation of our method against state-of-the-art competition in the low-dose CT image denoising area.

Recent successes in dialogue comprehension tasks are attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialogues as positive examples, forcing similar dialogues to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialogue representations from labeled and unlabeled dialogues. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-task learning framework for both tree construction and contrastive pre-training. To optimize efficiency, it implements a tree attention mechanism and a score function that considers both structural and textual information. To tackle class imbalance during training, it introduces a dynamic positive/negative ratio adjustment. Experimental results show that SPACE-2 achieves superior performance compared to monolithic and non-semi-supervised baselines in diverse dialogue comprehension tasks across four datasets.

This research aims to examine a hypothetical ideal fluid spacetime's geometric configuration in relation to its conformal Yamabe metric, specifically the Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first establish the link between the conformal Yamabe metric and the Yamabe metric in an ideal fluid spacetime. Next, we identify the conditions required for an ideal fluid spacetime to operate as a Ricci-Yamabe soliton. We then derive a scalar field equation that arises from the Ricci-Yamabe soliton condition, in addition to the Einstein field equations. Our analysis reveals that an ideal fluid spacetime's Ricci-Yamabe soliton can only occur when the fluid's energy density and pressure meet specific exponential relationships with the spacetime's conformal metric.

To study the distortion in halo nuclei, we utilize the angular momentum projection method on ground state and excited rotational modes. A novel phenomenon, shape uncoupling, is observed in the spectra of these nuclei. By comparing calculated spectra with experimental data, we find that the rotation around intrinsic shapes in dimensionless form is effective in describing rotational patterns. Moreover, our results indicate that the distortion in halo nuclei leads to increased intrinsic angular momentum and rotation frequency. This causes a shift from shape coupling to uncoupling and accelerates rotational motion. This research provides new evidence on the distortion of halo nuclei and its implications on nuclear shape uncoupling effects.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

This study proposes an efficient new method to estimate the energy of proton-proton collisions producing muons and Higgs bosons at the Large Hadron Collider. To accurately determine the energy of these events, our method utilizes several simultaneous measurements using leading jet momenta, forward forward measurements, and forward backward measurements. We demonstrate that this approach results in a more precise energy estimation compared to traditional methods, at a significantly lower computational cost. Additionally, our analysis introduces an innovative way to utilize data from the LHC, allowing for more efficient selection of events, which translates to a higher signal sensitivity in searches for additional high-energy particles.

In a reinforcement learning environment with multiple tasks, where task selection is unpredictable, the model-based multi-task reinforcement learning approach faces a significant challenge when tasks have distinct patterns but are closely linked, as the state visits are confounded due to the overlapping structure between tasks. As a result, the value function estimates become entangled, exacerbating the challenge of learning. To overcome this issue, we propose an innovative strategy of breaking the system into separate modules, where each module represents a subset of related tasks. Through numerical experiments and analyses, we demonstrate that this approach not only mitigates the adverse effects of interference but also accelerates learning by reducing the degree of entanglement. Moreover, we show that our method is computationally efficient compared to other multi-task reinforcement learning methods. In particular, we find that it achieves comparable performance in a single-task setting and outperforms existing multi-task methods by a significant margin when the tasks are highly overlapping. Additionally, we investigate the theoretical benefits of our method in terms of the rate of exploration and exploitation.

This paper investigates two types of partial differential equations - specifically the porous medium type and the rapid diffusion type - within a bounded, non-compact domain that becomes compact when bounded. The analysis is performed in a metric measure space, providing a broad framework that can accommodate both convex and non-convex equations. The study establishes a new approximation method using directional differentiable functions, facilitating existence and uniqueness proofs for the original equations. Additionally, this approach is shown to be computationally efficient and reliable.

In 1933, Kurt Godel and Alonzo Church were actively exchanging letters with J. Barkley Rosser, discussing the possibility of formulating a principle that would allow for the proof of consistency within any formal system. However, Godel passed away in 1975, long before I discovered these historical letters in 2001. Had Godel been alive, I would have liked to discuss his thoughts on this matter, as his opinions would have been incredibly valuable. Throughout this paper, I will examine the concepts that arose from Godel's influence, including his incompleteness theorems, Ullian truths, and the concept of a consistent formal system, as well as the opinions of other logicians with whom I have had the opportunity to converse.

This paper formulates three-sphere theorems for functions behaving according to Dirac's equation, utilizing techniques from complex variable theory. Specifically, we establish three-sphere theorems for functions that are analytic across certain complex planes within $\mathbb{R}^3$, as well as those that are analytic across three-spheres. These results can be generalized to apply to the Dirac operator in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The provided guidelines also outline a method for obtaining results analogous to Hartman's theorem.

When the population is not fully known in advance, the sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel technique for sequential geographically balanced sampling. The method recommends the next sample based on the current batch, ensuring that it maintains a balanced distribution mirroring the geographic characteristics of the entire population. If the suggested sample contains an unusual feature that is not present in the current population, it is confirmed by checking a secondary stratum. If it passes this check, it is included in the sample. If not, a new sample is drawn. The method is illustrated using real data from the US American Community Survey.

To facilitate versatile robotic grasping, having control over the camera and image interpretation system is crucial.  By regulating the camera and image processing, the target can be optimized for maximum identification, ultimately leading to improved object recognition and successful task execution. While significant progress has been made in modeling the relationship between the camera and image data, the standard approach relies on linear transformations derived from stereo vision, extrinsic parameters, and motion fields. However, this method has limitations in its extension to monocular vision due to the unknown scale factor.  Therefore, this paper focuses on developing a learning algorithm capable of determining the eye-in-hand camera position from a single image, with the aim of enhancing robotic tasks such as object recognition and state estimation.  After reviewing the existing methods and challenges in this field, this paper presents a novel algorithm based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) to predict the camera orientation and position directly from an image.  The algorithm's performance was evaluated using a custom dataset in an industrial setting, featuring various objects and showing promising results.

In scenarios where behavioral data is needed to solve mathematical optimization problems, such as inverse planning in radiation therapy, solving optimization problems is essential to generate relevant reference standards. Due to the high computational costs and limited computational resources on large scales, it is necessary to approximate the optimal solution by searching for certain posterior distributions. To achieve this, the search space needs to be refined by limiting the deviation of generated samples from certain references, thereby enhancing the efficiency of search algorithms. Therefore, a new method was proposed in this paper to achieve this by training a conditional generator that takes into account a regularization term to minimize the discrepancy between generated samples and their corresponding labels, thereby shaping the probability distribution of generated samples. To apply this method to real-world data, a convolutional conditional generator was designed and integrated with an efficient algorithm to learn the posterior distribution by limiting the deviation of generated samples in the training process. Experimental results showed that the proposed method outperformed existing techniques by a significant margin in accuracy when applied to real-world data in radiation therapy.

This article examines the notion of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems of a particular type and demonstrates that under specific conditions, surfaces of this kind cannot exist in a particular environment. To this end, we first define the appropriate context, including a dynamical system in a two-dimensional space with variables $x$ and $y$, where the system's evolution is described by equations involving the Alexits-Korenberg operator. We then establish that in order for an invariant surface to exist, a particular derivative must be constant along that surface, which in turn leads to the determination of constraints on the system's parameters under the given conditions. Specifically, when the Alexits-Korenberg operator is replaced by the Caputo operator, we show that certain parameters must be zero in order for an invariant surface to exist.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is characterized by very short communication distances due to extreme signal attenuation. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop technology to extend communication ranges, though optimizing beam training in such systems has become a significant challenge. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages reinforcement learning to develop an efficient strategy for enhancing beam training in multi-hop THz communication systems. The proposed method, utilizing a reinforcement learning algorithm, learns from environmental feedback to locate optimal alignment between transmitting and receiving devices, ultimately resulting in substantial increases in data transfer rates and overall system performance.

The line of sight to high-mass X-ray binary pulsars often contains a complex interstellar medium, which can comprise multiple scintillation components resulting from the intersection of the pulsar's radio beam with the medium's different structures. By examining the scintillation pattern of the pulsar B1133+16, researchers believe they have identified at least three distinct components along this line of sight. A statistical analysis of the scintillation pattern's orientation is presented, allowing researchers to infer the angle between two key components ranging from 33 degrees to 139 degrees. Furthermore, the finding of reduced scintillation bandwidth in B1133+16, particularly in the intermediate component, may indicate the presence of an interstellar structure with irregular boundaries, affecting the pulsar's scintillation pattern.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to input frequency parameters via dilated convolution layers with dynamic temporal resolution. Secondly, the model is optimized for quasi-periodic signal structures by stacking bilateral symmetric frequency layer components and includes an external periodic signal encoder in an attention-based cross-domain generation framework. Experimental evaluations of QPNet are conducted using the VCTK and VCSL corpora in terms of waveform and spectrum generation, demonstrating superior performance compared to the original WaveNet and a baseline model.

This research presents a novel web-based marking and editing tool called MADARi for Arabic words. The feature allows users to morphologically analyze Arabic words and edit spellings simultaneously. Based on the analysis, a thesaurus containing all possible word forms is generated. The tool incorporates multiple morphological analyses per word, enabling users to select the most appropriate analysis. It utilizes the Mander2 framework and integrates the TDF format with TIGRES. Furthermore, the tool includes a user-friendly interface that includes a cleaning feature to handle ambiguous and redundant analyses, as well as a filter for multiple analysis support.

As exoplanets are discovered at an incredible rate, the focus is shifting from detection to characterization. This process involves determining an exoplanet's composition and other properties using a variety of observational methods. Our research targets temperate exoplanets surrounded by thick atmospheres, which can hide the surface using heat generated by absorption of solar energy. We develop a new approach to analyze this atmosphere by studying the absorption patterns of the exoplanet as it moves in front of its star in a technique known as transit spectral mapping. This method is sensitive to the chemical composition and temperature structure of the atmosphere by mapping the absorption patterns across different wavelength ranges. Our team has been using this approach to study several exoplanets with atmospheres consisting of superstorms, high wind speeds, and layers of hot gases around massive stars. Additionally, we have been using this approach to study exoplanets around smaller stars, for which we can obtain more detailed data due to their larger size. Our analysis involves using multiple models to interpret the data, combining the results to create a final picture of the exoplanet's atmosphere, and evaluating the accuracy of our findings using statistics. Our ultimate goal is to extend this analysis to systems with multiple planets, which could provide insights into the effects of planetary interactions on atmospheric development.

The unique tunneling behavior of Majorana modes is based on a Vogl-Inoue formula, which describes the tunneling density of states as a sharp peak at the zero-energy point. However, this theory has limitations when considering its validity across all lead types.

The development of advanced materials in road construction has outpaced the innovation of technologies used for road maintenance. For example, while road surfaces made from asphalt and concrete have a typical lifespan of 5 to 7 years, the availability of cutting-edge technology not tailored to these surfaces is causing the effectiveness of their detection and management. In response to this challenge, researchers propose a novel system called RoadAtlas, consisting of a specialized sensor called the Atlas sensor and tailored machine learning algorithms. Designed to operate on various road surfaces, including asphalt, concrete, and gravel, RoadAtlas can automatically identify and record highway defect data, including images, locations, and descriptions. Furthermore, the system provides real-time defect detection, prioritization, and mapping functionality via a web interface, enabling efficient road maintenance planning and execution.

The concept of shadows was originally proposed as a simple bicategorical version of the classical idea of shadows in category theory. However, it has since become clear that this proposal requires refinement, particularly due to issues arising from the limitations of Gray's monoidal 2-categorical functor theorem. This paper presents an enhanced definition for shadows, one that utilizes a stronger form of bicategorical functor theorem. The enhanced definition is demonstrated to be a natural extension of the original concept, and it results in a more robust bicategorical framework that encompasses both the original definition and the concept of bicategorical tracks. This connection between shadows and tracks is shown to derive from the relationship between strong monoidal 2-functor mappings and track structures, which in turn gives rise to a broader category-theoretic principle. Additionally, this paper introduces the term "track-like" to describe any concept that can be represented as a combination of a family of spans subject to certain axioms analogous to those defining shadows. It is further demonstrated that the category of presheaves on a bicategory equipped with the structure of shadows forms a subcategory of the category of presheaves with tracks, and this connection is utilized to establish a connection between the categories of presheaves on a bicategory and its substructure.

To localize sound sources, the human brain employs a complex process that contrasts with the relatively simple method used for visual target localization. This study aims to advance computer systems' ability to determine the origin of single auditory sources by incorporating a key aspect of the human localization process. This involves developing a novel representation that ignores over-lapping sound sources and focuses on exclusive sound sources, which we refer to as "sound source islands". We utilize this representation to train a novel auditory source localization model, achieving superior performance when tested on datasets that include source overlap, particularly on difficult cases where sources overlap audibly.

Current Graph Neural Networks, based on Euclidean geometry, utilize convex combinations of node features to achieve invariance. However, they fall short in capturing the properties of non-Euclidean distance metrics, such as manifold and hyperbolic spaces. A new formulation of Graph Neural Networks is proposed, leveraging a Lorentzian geometry approach. This framework involves an expansion of the neural network in terms of Lorentzian polynomials, allowing for adaptations to diverse geometric contexts. Furthermore, a novel optimization strategy is proposed to tackle the challenge of computing node embeddings, drawing from the properties of Lorentzian polynomials. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate significant improvements in performance for GNNs. A specific application of the proposed method is also highlighted in the context of medical diagnosis, where a modified version of the method is employed to achieve accurate disease classification.

This research in inverse problems seeks to determine the acoustic properties of a medium based on structural vibration data. We take an approach, solving the direct problem through the use of finite element methods and a direct solver to accurately model structural and acoustic interactions. In the inverse problem, we employ a gradient-based optimization method to recover the medium's properties, utilizing boundary sensors' data to treat the problem as semi-overdetermined. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with simulations of a complex geometries and experiments using a structured sensor array.

A new method has been proposed that achieves the same outcome as an optical parametric oscillator, but using a different process. This process involves using a strong, continuous light source to drive the conversion of light photons into mechanical quanta within an optomechanical system. The model shows that a high ratio of mechanical quanta to photon numbers can be achieved, even when the system is operating in a steady-state condition. This is based on a hybrid optomechanical system design, where the interaction between the optomechanical cavity and an external reservoir is controlled. The parametric oscillation in this system is triggered by the continuous application of a strong, coherent light source. This leads to a steady-state condition where there is a constant conversion of photon pairs into mechanical quanta. The model also highlights the importance of quanta compression, which is achieved when the system is operated in a steady-state condition and there is a high ratio of mechanical quanta to photon numbers. This is accompanied by a reduction in the number of photon photons and a shift in the distribution of the system towards a cat state. The proposed model has the potential to be experimentally tested using current optomechanical systems.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets represented as relations over multiple variables. The focus lies on a simplified version of the formulae, denoted as $\mu\sigma$-calculus, which maintains equivalence to the original modal $\mu$-calculus but offers a more concise representation. Our discussion explores both the expressive capabilities and verification techniques of the $\mu\sigma$-calculus, covering its relationship to the modal $\mu$-calculus and its own tractable fragments, in addition to introducing a collaborative verification method for $\mu\sigma$-calculus formulae by students and a more complex, yet still expeditious, approach for the general case.

We propose an exponential discounting model incorporating
variations in timing bias and delay discounting, which serves as a
compass for analyzing the complex implications of these phenomena.
Initially, we break down individual components of the model, such as
its parameters and how they relate to standard discounting models.
We then investigate the model's parameters in an attempt to identify
its core properties and how they relate to established discounting
theories. Our research is an attempt to provide a clear perspective
on the complex issue of delay discounting.

We discuss harmonic gauge fixed point deceptions in massive gravity theory, explaining why they yield a non-metric tensor field, and demonstrate how a suitable redefinition of the harmonic gauge field leads to a fourth degree covariant equation. Additionally, we show that the helicity zero mode of the tensor field is propagating in some harmonic gauge theories.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with the idea of extended double covers. We are investigating the basic properties and characteristics of this combination of concepts, known as extended double covers of signed graphs. Our research focuses particularly on how the polarity assigned to the edges affects the structure and characteristics of these combined entities. We are examining whether certain properties or characteristics of a signed graph can be determined by examining a specific subset of the graph, known as a homomorphism limit. Our results show that certain properties or characteristics of a signed graph can be completely determined by analyzing a specific subset of the graph, while others cannot be accurately determined by analyzing that subset alone. We are also investigating the relationship between these properties or characteristics and other properties or characteristics of graph theory.

In 1935, H. Weyl and J. von Neumann independently reached the conclusion that a canonical transformation cannot be represented by a unitary transformation over an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. This limitation is addressed by an alternative approach using Weyl-Wigner transforms, which enable the expression of canonical transformations in the form of Weyl-Wigner series. This approach is utilized to reexamine the conditions that lead to thermal equilibrium in quantum systems, thereby providing a more general framework that encompasses both unitary and Weyl-Wigner transforms. The resulting statistics, which we refer to as canonical equilibrium conditions, depend on the Weyl-Wigner transforms and are formulated in a way that enables the derivation of thermal correlations and densities. Our study also reveals that the symmetry characteristic of Weyl-Wigner transforms, which is related to the Weyl-Wigner symbol of the annihilation operator, leads to a specific mean value, which is constant and unaffected by the temperature, thereby displaying the system's infinite temperature behavior.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been firmly established as a valid idea with numerous applications across physics fields. As a result, the initial skepticism that existed among physicists has dissipated, revealing opportunities for further research and discovery. In this discussion, some of the promising developments stemming from the notion of negative absolute temperature will be discussed, set against the backdrop of the remarkable journey the scientific community has embarked upon since the 1990s.

We investigate the basic question of finding the fewest nonnegative integers at least one in a finite set of real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ whose sums with sign configurations add up to a given number, in the range of conjecture and certainty. In the case of equal sums, we prove a corresponding result about the minimum number of integers required. Additionally, we address related questions on Gaussian sums and the sums of nonnegative numbers with specific properties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histologically is crucial to determine patient risk and appropriate treatment. Traditionally, diagnosis relies on histological analysis by experienced pathologists. However, this process can be time-consuming and may lead to diagnostic discrepancies between different experts. To complement and assist pathologists in daily practice, computer-aided diagnosis tools have been proposed using deep learning techniques. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive dataset of stained tissue samples, UniToPatho, which comprises 9530 annotated regions spanning various patterns of normal, benign, and malignant colorectal polyps, including various degrees of adenoma dysplasia. This dataset serves as a resource to develop and evaluate deep learning-based approaches for classifying polyps and predicting the severity of adenoma dysplasia.

This research proposes a versatile numerical method for solving high-frequency scattering problems, specifically those involving smooth variations in material properties. The proposed scheme combines a novel boundary element method with a technique for solving a weak form of the boundary integral equation, utilizing a finite element mesh that can accommodate non-matching interfaces. The implementation of this method is shown on several examples, including problems with overlapping sub-domains, deliberately aliased images, and complex structures such as a car undergoing scattering. Compared to other numerical methods, this method shows comparable results in terms of accuracy but has the advantage of minimal storage requirements.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in two stony meteorites, Chelyabinsk and Benenitra. Our research indicates these meteorites have similar ratios of water to hydrogen, suggesting the presence of hydroxyl groups within their mineral structures. This is in contrast to previous findings on the LL3.0 meteorite group, which showed varying water to hydrogen ratios. We considered potential sources of water accumulation, including solar nebula, planetary environments, and planetesimal orbits. However, their similar isotopic compositions and existing records of Antarctic meteorites suggest they accumulated water during orbital journeys through the inner solar system. Existing models of planet formation also support the idea that planetesimals with high water content could have survived intense solar radiation. Therefore, we believe our findings provide novel evidence for the accumulation of water through gas-solid reactions during the planet formation process.

Using an exact-correlation approach, all single-site form factors for higher-spin XXZ chains are determined, and this method is shown to be applicable to attain affine quantum-algebra symmetry. The approach relies on the integer-index property of the XXZ chain's Hamiltonian and correlation matrix, which is combinatorially solved through the transfer-matrix method, facilitated by the Frobenius-Percy duality. The symmetry is then established through the 11-theorem. The determinants of the form factors yield eigenvalues that match known results for the XXZ chain at its critical point, and also confirm the central charge $c=1$ value as derived from the thermodynamic Bethe-ansatz equation.

Language barriers pose significant challenges in international settings, where people who speak different languages may need to communicate with each other. Interpretation and translation fill this communication gap, although they have distinct purposes - interpretation conveys the spoken word, while translation changes written language into another language. Despite the advancements in machine translation, little research has focused on translating spoken language. This task is further complicated by the absence of parallel data, a necessary resource for traditional translation models. We introduce a novel task called zero-shot voice translation, which involves translating spoken language into a target language the model hasn't been exposed to. To achieve this, we've developed a framework that combines two models - a voice translation model and a language model. This framework allows zero-shot translation by leveraging the general knowledge of the combined models. However, it doesn't guarantee perfect understanding of the spoken input by the model. To overcome this challenge, we utilized speech-to-text to convert spoken language into text, which can then be translated by the model. We've also investigated different speech recognition and translation models, as well as evaluated our framework on zero-shot voice translation.

We introduce local multilocal field approximations, expanding on the traditional linear susceptibility model. This new method goes beyond the long wavelength approximation and is applicable to complex systems featuring multiple types of scatterers. We then develop a general formula for determining the multilocal fields within a specific region by considering the interactions of scatterers both within and outside that area. This formula can be specifically tailored to account for local intensities, polarization fields, and other field parameters. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach by comparing it to the traditional methods and evaluating its accuracy with regard to relevant physical constraints. Furthermore, we introduce numerical techniques for calculating the multilocal fields through direct optimization and by utilizing the available software, EMA3D.

Building on the concept of quantum immanents, this study introduces a new set of polynomial functions called the quantum altered Schur functions. These functions can be defined through double Young-Capelli bitableaux, an extension of the Capelli operators initially presented by Kostant. The altered Schur functions have a more compact representation of tableaux compared to the original Schur functions and the changed tableaux are similar to the atypical partitions identified by Brion. The study demonstrates the relationship between the altered Schur functions and the quantum immanents through specific operator presentations and shows that the altered Schur functions can be expressed with the quantum altered Schur functions as their equivariant counterpart. The study also reveals that the altered Schur functions can be defined with the use of the extended Nazarov-Zhelobenko subalgebra and its central part, and that these functions are connected to the original Schur functions through the dual map.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the implications for dark matter and Higgs vacuum stability. Initially, we introduce three new scalar fields associated with the dark sector and investigate their interaction within the context of the standard model. Subsequently, we determine the parameter regions that satisfy the condition for dark matter stability and meet the necessary criteria for a viable phenomenological description. Concurrently, we investigate the conditions under which the standard model remains stable, and identify the relevant constraints. The model exhibits viability at low energy scales, and dark matter mass values of approximately 1 TeV. Furthermore, we find that the model's stability requirements can be satisfied with energy scales exceeding 5 TeV, thus demonstrating the model's ability to ensure the stability of the standard model within its own energy range.

We employ exact diagonalization on the cubic basis to study the breakdown of
$t_{2g}$ symmetry in 4d and 5d transition metal compounds. By directly comparing
$t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ energy levels, we identify the point at which the distinction
blurs, characterizing the large-scale effect on $d$-orbital coupling. Our analysis
reveals that the spectral weight transferred during $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing causes
heavy electrons in 4d compounds and heavy quasi-particles in 5d compounds. This
analysis is followed by a discussion of this effect's influence on the density
of states and the localization length of heavy quasi-particles.

This study examines how relative quantum topological invariants change under a specific type of algebraic modification called birational alteration. We demonstrate that the refined Chern-Simons invariant exhibits continuity when the base field is altered in a way that preserves the field's properties. Moreover, we establish that the refined Chern-Simons invariant remains conserved when the variety undergoes certain types of algebraic transformations. This research extends previous findings related to absolute quantum topological invariants, building on previous work by Mu\'noz, Niebuhr, and the author.

The accuracy of AI models using chest X-rays for lung disease detection relies heavily on their ability to process high-quality images. Since X-ray images can be distorted or obscured by various marks, it's essential to develop techniques to enhance their clarity and reliability. While current advances in image processing have focused on restoring aesthetic appeal, little work has been done on adapting these techniques to detect underlying conditions associated with image defects. Building on previous research, this paper expands on that foundation by exploring new approaches to detecting condition-related abnormalities in chest X-rays. Four different datasets are used to test these methods, and the results show they can be 5-10% more accurate than traditional detection models.

ViDaExpert is a data visualization tool designed for in-depth analysis of multi-dimensional vector data in nonlinear visualization. It allows users to easily create high-dimensional data plots, comparing their methodology to established algorithms for t-SNE and Multi-Dimensional Scaling. Additionally, it features an interactive interface for manual data manipulation and filtering techniques, including pairwise distance calculation, mean centering, and variance normalization, all accessible through a data explorer interface. ViDaExpert is available as an open-source R package for users and researchers.

This research paper proposes a method for quickly estimating cancer cell invasion potential using a simple mathematical model applied to 2D flat domains. The authors utilize a range of mathematical techniques, including linear stability analysis and boundary value problem solutions, to understand how their model behaves over time. They then develop a straightforward way to calculate the steepness of parabolic points on their domain without solving the entire boundary value problem. The accuracy of their method is validated using simulated data and observed to be comparable to more sophisticated techniques. The authors also examine the factors that affect invasion time, suggesting that their approach offers a useful tool for understanding the types of domains that promote stable coexistence between cancer cells and healthy cells.
